newsitem.title: INDIA: FEATURE-India's tyre industry skidding into trouble.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-India's tyre industry skidding into trouble.

text.p: When foreign car makers first started rolling into India, Indian tyre firms were among the first to uncork the bubbly.
Secure in the knowledge that they stood at the heart of one of the world's fastest growing car markets, they feverishly expanded capacity.
Five years later, they are wringing their hands.
RISING TIDE OF ECONOMIC REFORM
Ironically, it is the rising tide of economic reform, which earlier promised to lift the sector, that now threatens to swamp it.

Foreign car companies were given permission to set up shop in India under an economic reforms programme, launched in 1991, which swept away decades of socialist controls and invited private and foreign investors.
In the same spirit of liberalisation, India announced in April 1997 it was dismantling half a century of barriers to foreign tyre imports and allowing both new and used tyres to be imported freely.
The announcement silenced Indian tyre makers who had been whooping with joy in the earlier phases of liberalisation.

"How can a $440 million Indian company compete with a $14 billion American tyre company?" one senior official at an Indian tyre firm lamented. "It's a question of unequal competition and economies of scale."
Tyre industry officials say they are worried that used tyres from other countries will soon flood the Indian market.
"Earlier, used tyres used to be burnt. But now environmental groups are stepping up pressure, so they will be dumped in markets like ours," one official said.
"For them it is waste, so it will be sold very cheaply here. Who will buy our tyres then? It will completely disrupt the market."
FOREIGN TYRE MAKERS EYEING FAST-GROWING MARKET
India's car production grew by 16 percent to 404,040 vehicles in 1996/97 (April-March), and by 32 percent in the previous year.
The Association of Indian Automobile Manufacturers projects car production at 850,000 vehicles by the year 2001.

Large Western car companies such as Mercedes-Benz AG, Peugeot SA, General Motors Corp unit Adam Opel, Bayerische Motoren Werke AG, Fiat Spa and Volkswagen AG are either already in India or considering entering it.
Asian players eyeing India or already established there include Daewoo Motor, Honda Motor Co Ltd, Mitsubishi Motors Corp, Toyota Motor Corp, Hyundai Motor Co and Suzuki Motor Corp.
Tyre industry officials say they are worried that most foreign firms will use radial-ply tyres on their cars, which few Indian tyre makers produce.

Only about 30 percent of India's car tyres are radials -- the bulk have traditional cross-ply treads which are well suited for bumpy Indian roads but have shorter lives than radial tyres that are likely to be sold second-hand and dirt cheap in India.
INDIAN TYRE MAKERS ALREADY HAVE HANDS FULL
Industry officials say there are already far too many tyre makers jostling for space in a small, crowded market.
Apart from nearly a dozen local tyre makers, Goodyear Tire and Rubber Co, Bridgestone Corp and Michelin are trying to get a grip over the Indian market through local subsidiaries.
"The biggest problem Apollo faces is how to reach an ever increasing customer base faster than the competition," said Apollo Tyres Ltd spokesman Deepak Mukarji.

Some tyre firms are already in serious trouble. Analysts say Dunlop India's 1989/90 market share of 15 percent dwindled to about one percent in 1996/97 after a battle among top managers exacerbated the cash-strapped company's problems.

The Automotive Tyre Manufacturers Association says Indian tyre makers' output grew by 40 percent to 27.89 million tyres in 1995/96 from 19.95 million tyres in 1992/93. In the first 10 months of 1996/97, production crossed 27 million.

Tyre makers grumble that rubber is expensive on the domestic market while foreign tyre firms can benefit from purchases at competitive international prices. Rubber imports into India require special licences, which they say are hard to come by.

Rubber Board of India officials say a domestic rubber supply gap of 31,000 tonnes in 1996/97 will widen dramatically to 319,000 tonnes by 2010/11, and are urging planters to put more land under cultivation.
TYRE DEALERS SAY MANUFACTURERS CHICKEN-HEARTED
Tyre dealers say domestic manufacturers are kicking up a fuss over imports simply to shield themselves from competition and maintain a stranglehold over the Indian market.

"In the last five decades, the domestic tyre cartel has exploited the market through high price rigging, carrying on with outdated, high cost cross-ply technology and unethical trade practices," said All India Tyre Dealers' Federation convenor S.P. Singh.
He said the government had progressively slashed excise duty on tyres and import tariffs on raw materials.
"But the track record of domestic tyre makers due to the monopoly situation has been to pocket the tax benefits by holding the captive home market to ransom," Singh said.
"The efforts of domestic tyre giants to pre-empt imports is nothing but a panicky reaction as they are wary of genuine global competition."
